unit.title: Perform basic welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW) - Fuel Gas Welding

summary: This unit is about oxy-acetylene welding (OAW) at Level 3: planning gas welding jobs to a procedure, running a safe gas supply, and choosing the method, flame, nozzle and filler for each job. You will weld steel sheet, plate and small-bore pipe by the leftward and rightward methods in different positions, deal with cast iron, aluminium and coated steel, control distortion, and inspect, test and record the work while supervising other welders.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). You already know how to set up a gas set and weld thin sheet. At Level 3 you **plan** gas welding jobs, write or check the **welding procedure (WPS)**, choose between methods, weld thicker plate and pipe in more positions, handle metals other than mild steel, and **lead and check** the work of others.

Oxy-acetylene welding is slower than arc welding and puts more heat into the job, but it needs no electricity, the equipment is portable, and the welder controls heat and filler separately. That makes it the right choice for thin sheet, small-bore pipe, repairs in the field, some cast iron work, and jobs where the same set is used for heating, brazing and cutting.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees who can already set up an oxy-acetylene set and weld mild steel sheet safely, and who will now plan, lead and check gas welding work in workshops and on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Plan the job
Read the drawing and weld symbols, write or check a WPS, work out gas, filler and time, and brief the team.
Run a safe gas supply
Handle, store and couple cylinders correctly, and keep acetylene within its safe pressure and flow.
Check and maintain the equipment
Test regulators, hoses, arrestors and torches for leaks and faults, and take faulty parts out of use.
Light up, shut down and act in an emergency
Follow the safe sequences, and deal correctly with backfires, flashbacks and fires.
Choose and set the flame
Set neutral, carburising and oxidising flames and know which job each is for.
Weld by the right method and position
Use leftward and rightward welding on sheet, plate and small-bore pipe in the flat, horizontal, vertical and overhead positions.
Weld other metals and control distortion
Weld or braze-weld cast iron, weld aluminium and coated steel safely, and keep the job in shape.
Inspect, test, supervise and record
Inspect and test welds, coach trainees, and keep weld, job and incident records.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, procedures, calculations, gas supply, equipment, flames, technique, positions, pipe, other metals, distortion, testing, defects, supervision and records.
A **written paper** with short answers and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practicals**: rightward single-V butt welds in 8 mm plate to a group-written WPS, with bend tests and a report; and a thin-sheet tray made to a job plan with distortion control and a leak test.

blocks.note: Level 3 questions often give you a situation and ask what the team leader should do. Think in this order: is it safe, does it follow the procedure, and how will I check and record it?
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A WPS works only if it is followed. If a welder changes the nozzle, the method or the rod, the weld is no longer the one the procedure proved, even if it looks good. The team leader has it re-welded to the WPS, or asks the person responsible to review the WPS.

flow: Read the drawing and order: metal, thickness, joints, sizes, quantity, finish
Write or check the WPS: method, nozzle, pressures, flame, rod, tacking and welding order
Work out the gas, filler rod and time needed; check stock and order more
Plan jigs and clamps for repeat parts, and the steps to control distortion
Check the site: what is behind and under the work that could burn; ventilation; access
Check every gas set before work; give out tasks and brief the team on the WPS and safety
Check the first part fully against the drawing before the rest are made
Check during the work; record checks, gas used and problems at the end

head: Sum
Example
rows: Gas used
Nozzle using 400 litres of acetylene an hour × 3.5 hours = **1 400 litres**
Gas cost
1 500 litres of oxygen at J$2 = J$3 000, plus 1 400 litres of acetylene at J$5 = J$7 000; total **J$10 000**
Welding time
A 900 mm seam at 75 mm a minute: 900 ÷ 75 = **12 minutes**
Filler rod
0.2 kg of rod a metre × 24 m of weld = **4.8 kg**
Pressure units

blocks.note: A neutral flame takes oxygen and acetylene from the cylinders in about **equal volumes** (oxygen slightly more). So for gas planning, the oxygen used is roughly the same as the acetylene used. The rest of the oxygen the flame needs comes from the air.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn fiercely. Oil, grease and clothing soaked with oxygen can burst into flame. Oxygen cylinders are filled to a very high pressure (often about 200 bar).

ul: Never let oil or grease touch oxygen fittings, regulators or valves, and never handle them with oily gloves.
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or benches, to cool yourself or to "freshen" the air.
Never use oxygen in place of compressed air to drive tools.

blocks.p: Acetylene gives the hottest flame of the common fuel gases, which is why it is used for fusion welding of steel. But **free acetylene under pressure is unstable**: above about 1 bar (15 psi) it can break down and explode on its own, without any air. So it is stored **dissolved in acetone**, soaked into a porous mass that fills the cylinder.

ul: Never set the acetylene working pressure above the limit on the regulator and the supplier's instructions (about 1 bar, 15 psi).
Use and store acetylene cylinders **upright**, so acetone is not drawn out with the gas. If one has been lying down, stand it upright for the time the supplier gives before use.

Acetylene forms explosive compounds with **copper**, silver and mercury. Fittings and pipes in contact with acetylene must not be copper or high-copper alloys (above about 70% copper). Never make up acetylene pipework or manifolds from copper pipe.
Acetone drawn out with the gas shows as a purple tinge in the flame. It damages the equipment and the weld.

blocks.h: How fast you can draw acetylene

blocks.p: Acetylene comes out of the acetone only so fast. Suppliers set a **maximum withdrawal rate**, often about **one-seventh of the cylinder's contents per hour** for continuous use (follow your supplier's figure). Drawing faster pulls acetone out, and the flame and the weld suffer.

blocks.note: **Cylinders needed = flow the nozzle needs ÷ the safe flow from one cylinder, rounded up.** Example: a heating nozzle needs 1 500 litres an hour; each cylinder holds about 6 000 litres; one-seventh is about 860 litres an hour; 1 500 ÷ 860 = 1.7, so **2 cylinders** must be coupled.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When one cylinder is not enough, two or more are joined on an approved **manifold**: a header with a flexible pigtail, a non-return valve and a flashback arrestor for each cylinder, and one regulator feeding the line. A manifold is supplied and installed as a complete approved system, never made up in the workshop.

ul: Keep cylinders **upright and secured** with chains or straps on a trolley, rack or wall.
Move them on a cylinder trolley, valves closed, caps or guards fitted. Never roll, drag or drop them, or lift them by the valve.
Store full and empty cylinders apart and labelled, in a cool, dry, ventilated place out of the sun.
Keep oxygen apart from fuel gas cylinders by a safe distance (often about 6 m) or a fire-resisting wall, as the Centre's rules say.
Carry cylinders to a site upright and secured, valves closed, in a ventilated vehicle, never in a closed car boot.
Cylinder colours differ between suppliers and standards: always read the **label**, never go by colour alone.

sections.title: Equipment: regulators, hoses, arrestors and torches

head: Part
What it does
What to know
rows: Regulator
Lowers cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
**Single-stage**: the working pressure drifts as the cylinder empties and must be reset
**Two-stage**: holds the pressure steady as the cylinder empties; better for long jobs
Oxygen and fuel gas regulators are different and never swapped
Gauges
Show cylinder (contents) pressure and working pressure
Glass not cracked; needles return to zero when the pressure is off
Hoses
Carry gas to the torch
Red for fuel gas; blue (or green in the American system) for oxygen
Fuel gas nuts have a **left-hand thread** and a groove or notch; oxygen nuts are right-hand. They cannot be mixed up
Repair only with proper hose fittings and ferrules; replace damaged hose; never join with pipe and screw clips or tape
**Flashback arrestor**
Fitted at each regulator outlet
A **flame-stop element** puts out a flame trying to pass back through it
A **non-return valve** stops gas flowing back up the hose
Many also have a **cut-off valve** that shuts if the arrestor gets hot
After a flashback, check or replace it as the maker says
Hose check valves
Fitted at the torch inlets
Stop gases mixing back into the hoses
Torch
Mixes the gases and burns them at the nozzle
**Equal-pressure (high-pressure) torch**: both gases arrive at about the same pressure and meet in the **mixing chamber**
**Injector (low-pressure) torch**: a fast jet of oxygen draws the fuel gas through, so it works with a low fuel pressure
Nozzles
Set the size of the flame
Sizes are chosen from the **maker's chart** for the metal thickness, with the matching pressures
Each maker numbers nozzles its own way: use the chart for the torch you have
Clean with the right tip cleaner, straight in and out

blocks.h: Checking a set for leaks and faults

flow: Check every part by eye: no oil, damage, cracked gauges or worn hoses; arrestors in date and fitted the right way
Open the cylinder valves slowly and set the working pressures; close the torch valves
Brush **leak-test solution** (or soapy water) on every joint from the cylinder valves to the torch; bubbles mean a leak
**Drop test:** close the cylinder valves and watch the gauges for a few minutes. A falling cylinder-pressure gauge means a leak between the cylinder and the regulator, or in the regulator
**Creep test:** with the torch valves shut, the working-pressure gauge should stay still. If it keeps rising, the regulator seat is letting gas by (creep)
Fix leaks only by tightening or replacing parts as trained; never use oil, tape or sealant on gas fittings

blocks.note: A regulator that creeps, a gauge that will not return to zero, a hose with a cut, a cracked nozzle or an arrestor that has stopped a flashback is **taken out of use at once**, tagged DO NOT USE with the date and the fault, kept where no one can pick it up, and reported in writing.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Safe working, lighting up, shutting down and emergencies

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Fire
Clear or cover anything that burns within about 10 m, including above and below
Check behind and under the work: fuel tanks and lines, wiring, wooden floors
Extinguisher at hand; fire watch during and after
Explosion
Never weld or heat containers that held fuel or chemicals until made safe by a competent person
Keep acetylene pressure within the limit
Find leaks with leak-test solution, **never with a flame**
Burns
Flame-resistant clothing, gauntlet gloves, boots
Tongs for hot work; mark hot work HOT
Never hang a lit torch on a cylinder or trolley; shut it off when you put it down
Eye damage
Gas welding goggles or face shield with filter **shade about 4–6** (darker for heavier work), from the chart
Arc welding shades are far too dark for gas work, and clear glasses give no protection from the glare
Fumes and gases
The flame makes carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides and uses up oxygen; ventilate small rooms
Coatings (zinc, paint, oil) give off harmful fume: remove them and use extraction
Oxygen enrichment
Check for oxygen leaks; never use oxygen for ventilation or cleaning

flow: Check the set and the area; goggles and gloves on
Open the cylinder valves slowly: oxygen fully; acetylene about ¾ to 1½ turns, with the key left on the valve so it can be shut quickly
Set the working pressures from the nozzle chart
**Purge** each hose separately for a few seconds, in a ventilated place away from flames, to clear air or mixed gas from the hoses
Open the acetylene torch valve a little and light it at once with a **spark lighter**, never a match or a cigarette lighter
Open the acetylene until the flame just stops smoking
Open the oxygen slowly until the flame is set as the job needs
Close the torch valves in the maker's order
Close both cylinder valves
Bleed each hose through the torch until the gauges read zero, then close the torch valves
Wind out the regulator adjusting screws
Coil the hoses, hang up the torch, check the area for anything smouldering

head: Event
What happens
Common causes
What to do
rows: Backfire (pop)
The flame goes out with a bang, and may relight
Nozzle touching the work or the pool, overheated or dirty nozzle, pressures too low, loose nozzle
Shut off, find the cause, clean or cool the nozzle, check pressures, relight
Sustained backfire
The flame burns back inside the torch with a squeal or hiss; the handle gets hot
As above, worse
Close the torch **oxygen** valve at once, then the fuel valve; let it cool; check the torch before re-use
Flashback
The flame burns back into the hoses or regulator
Gases mixed in a hose, faulty check valves, no arrestors
Close **both cylinder valves** if safe; check or replace arrestors, hoses and regulators before re-use

blocks.p: If an acetylene cylinder gets hot (after a flashback or a fire nearby), it can break down inside and explode, even some time later.

flow: Shut the cylinder valve, only if it is safe to reach
Clear everyone from the area and keep them well back
Call the fire service (in Jamaica, dial 110) and tell them it is an acetylene cylinder
Do not move the cylinder; if trained and safe, cool it with water spray from behind cover
Leave it to the fire service and the supplier to say when it is safe

blocks.p: Acetylene burns in two stages. In the **inner cone**, acetylene burns with the oxygen from the cylinder (about one volume of oxygen to one of acetylene) to make carbon monoxide and hydrogen. This is where the heat is greatest: about **3 100–3 200 °C** just in front of the cone tip. In the **outer envelope**, the carbon monoxide and hydrogen burn with oxygen from the **surrounding air** to make carbon dioxide and water vapour.

Burning one volume of acetylene completely needs about 2½ volumes of oxygen: about one from the cylinder and about 1½ from the air. The zone just in front of the inner cone has no free oxygen, so it protects the pool. That is why you hold the cone tip about 2–3 mm from the pool and keep the outer envelope over the hot metal.

head: Flame
How it looks
Effect on steel
Used for
rows: **Neutral** (about equal oxygen and acetylene)
Clear, rounded inner cone; no feather; quiet
Clean, fluid pool; adds nothing
Most welding of steel, cast iron and copper
**Carburising** (excess acetylene)
White feather round the inner cone; the longer the feather, the more excess
Adds carbon: the pool boils, the weld is hard and brittle
Hardfacing (a feather about two to three times the cone length, as the rod maker says); some aluminium work
**Oxidising** (excess oxygen)
Short, sharp, pointed inner cone; harsh hissing
Burns the steel: sparking, foaming pool, porous, brittle weld
Slightly oxidising for braze welding with brass or bronze rod, to cut zinc fuming; never for fusion welding steel

ul: Set a neutral flame by starting carburising and adding oxygen until the feather **just** merges into the inner cone. Adding oxygen past that point makes it oxidising.

Check the flame during long welds. If it drifts oxidising without you touching the valves, the acetylene supply is usually falling off: the cylinder is emptying, a single-stage regulator is drifting, or the draw is too high.

A **soft** flame (low gas speed) is easy to control but backfires easily; a **harsh** flame (high gas speed) blows the pool about. Choose the nozzle size for the job and set the pressures from the chart, rather than forcing a small nozzle.

blocks.note: Many welders judge the flame by the pool as well as by the cone. A bright, quiet, fluid pool means neutral; a boiling, cloudy pool means too much acetylene; sparks and foam mean too much oxygen.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Directions are given for a right-handed welder: torch in the right hand, rod in the left.

head: Point
Leftward (forehand)
Rightward (backhand)
rows: Direction of travel
Right to left
Left to right
Flame points
Ahead of the weld, onto the cold metal
Back over the weld just made
Rod
In front of the flame, dipped into the front of the pool
Behind the flame, between the flame and the finished weld
Movement
Torch moved steadily with a slight side-to-side weave; rod dipped in and out
Torch moved steadily along with no weave; rod makes small loops in the pool
Typical angles
Torch about 60–70° to the work; rod about 30–40°
Torch about 40–50° to the work; rod about 30–40°
Thickness
Sheet and thin plate, up to about 6 mm
Plate over about 6 mm, and pipe walls
Edge preparation for butt welds
Square edges with a gap on sheet; about 80° V on 3–6 mm
About 60° V on thicker plate (narrower, so less metal to fill)
Main advantages
Small, easily controlled pool; low risk of burning through thin sheet
Better view of the root; deeper fusion; less gas and rod on thick plate; the flame shields the weld so it cools more slowly; less distortion

blocks.h: Edge preparation for butt welds in steel (typical)

head: Thickness
Preparation
Method
rows: Up to about 1.5 mm
**Flanged edges**: each edge turned up a little (about one to two times the thickness) and melted down without filler
Leftward
About 1.5–3 mm
Square edges, gap about half the thickness
Leftward
About 3–5 mm
Single-V, about 80° included
Leftward
About 5 mm and over
Single-V, about 60° included, with root face and gap
Rightward

blocks.note: These are typical guides from gas welding practice. The WPS gives the preparation for your job. A common rule of thumb for rod size is about **half the plate thickness plus 1 mm** for leftward welding, and about **half the thickness** for rightward. A rod that is too thick chills the pool and leaves poor fusion; one that is too thin melts off in drops before it reaches the pool.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Position
Technique
rows: Flat
Easiest: the pool sits level. Use it whenever the job can be turned
Horizontal (on a vertical surface)
Flame angled slightly upward; rod fed at the **top** of the pool, so the pool does not sag onto the lower plate
Vertical
Usually welded **upward**, so the pool rests on the weld already made below; small pool; on thin sheet the joint may be closed with no V
Overhead
Keep the pool **small** and well under control; small nozzle; short, quick dips of rod; full PPE with neck and head covered

ul: Heat flows away into both plates of a fillet weld, so it needs a little more heat than a butt weld in the same thickness.
Aim more of the flame at the plate that takes heat away faster: the **thicker** plate, or the bottom plate of a lap joint, whose edge does not melt as easily as the top plate's thin edge.
Make sure the pool wets both plates and the root before you add rod.
Cut the ends square, bevel them if the wall needs it, and clean inside and out to bright metal.
Line the pipes up straight with an even gap, and tack in three or four places spaced evenly round the joint, so the gap and line stay even all round.
**Roll the pipe** whenever you can, so most of the joint is welded on top, in the flat. It is quicker and fuses more easily.
If the pipe is **fixed horizontal (5G)**, weld in two halves, each from just past the bottom, up over the top; overlap the starts and finishes.
Watch for full penetration at the bottom, where the weld is overhead.
Start by melting a pool in both edges before adding rod.
To restart, reheat the end of the weld until it melts, then carry on; never start a new pool beside the old one.
At the end, fill the crater and draw the flame away slowly, so the end does not crack or take in air.

blocks.p: A gas flame is far less concentrated than an arc. It heats the metal slowly and spreads heat over a wide band before the joint melts. A wider strip expands, then shrinks as it cools, and pulls the job out of shape. Gas welds also have a **wider heat-affected zone** than arc welds on the same metal. Thin sheet suffers most.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Close, even tacks
Hold the edges in line; on long seams tack from the middle outwards in a planned order
Tapered gap
On a long butt seam, set the gap wider at the far end, because the gap closes up as the weld moves along
Presetting
Set the parts slightly the opposite way, so the shrinking weld pulls them straight
Clamps and jigs
Hold the parts while they cool; a jig also makes repeat parts the same
**Chill bars**
Copper or steel bars clamped beside the seam draw heat away and narrow the hot band
Back-step or skip welding
Weld short lengths in a planned order, so heat is not built up in one place
Smallest suitable nozzle; steady speed
Less heat into the job, still with full fusion

blocks.p: Small distortion left after welding can be corrected. **Planishing** is hammering the weld and the metal beside it on a dolly or flat stake to stretch the shrunk area back. **Heat shrinking** is heating small spots or short lines on the stretched (bulging) area to a dull red and letting them cool, so they shrink and pull the panel flat. Use only as much heat as needed, and let it cool in air.
Grey cast iron is brittle: it cracks if it is heated or cooled unevenly. Fusion welding it with gas is done like this:

flow: Clean off oil and dirt; find the full length of the crack (dye penetrant helps)
Drill a small hole just beyond each end of the crack, so the crack cannot run further
Grind a V along the crack so the weld can reach the bottom
Preheat the whole part, or a wide area, slowly and evenly (often to about a dull red for fusion welding, or as the procedure says)

Weld with a **cast iron rod** and **cast iron flux** (the oxide on cast iron melts at a higher temperature than the iron), using a **neutral** or very slightly carburising flame; never oxidising, which burns out the carbon
Cool **very slowly**: bury the part in dry sand or lime, or cover it with a heat blanket, or let it cool in a furnace

blocks.p: **Braze welding** with bronze (brass) rod and flux is often chosen instead. It melts only the rod, at a much lower temperature (roughly 870–900 °C), so the casting needs less preheat and is less likely to crack. Use a **slightly oxidising** flame, which cuts zinc fuming from the rod, and "tin" the surfaces before building up. Braze welding is not suitable where the part runs hot or where the colour must match.

ul: Aluminium melts at about 660 °C, but its oxide skin melts at about 2 050 °C. A **flux** dissolves the oxide so the metal can fuse.
Aluminium **does not change colour** before it melts: watch for the surface to go glossy and wet, and be ready for it to collapse suddenly.
Use a neutral or very slightly carburising flame and aluminium filler rod; support the work, because it goes soft before it melts.
**Wash every trace of flux off** with hot water and a brush as soon as the job is done. Flux left on takes up moisture and corrodes the aluminium.
Most aluminium welding is now done by TIG or MIG, but gas welding is still used for small repairs.

blocks.p: Zinc boils off at a much lower temperature than steel melts. Its fume causes **metal fume fever** (flu-like chills and fever a few hours later) and gives porous welds. Grind or remove the zinc from the weld area first, use fume extraction, and repair the coating afterwards with zinc-rich paint.

head: Look at
A sound weld
rows: Face
Even width and height, smooth even ripples, filled crater; no undercut, cracks, holes, burnt metal or overlap
Root (underside)
Even penetration along the whole length: not missing, not excessive, no burn-through
The job
Parts in line, square, within size; little distortion

head: Defect
Main causes
Cure
rows: Lack of root penetration
Gap too small or root face too thick; nozzle too small; travel too fast; flame not aimed into the root
Fit up to the WPS; correct nozzle; watch for the small keyhole at the root
Lack of side fusion
Rod added before the edges melted; flame not playing on both edges
Melt both edges first; correct angles
Porosity
Oxidising flame; dirty rod or plate; flame lifted away so the pool is left open to the air
Neutral flame; clean metal; keep the envelope over the pool, also at the end
Burnt (oxidised) weld
Oxidising flame; too much heat
Reset to neutral; correct nozzle
Undercut
Too much heat and too little filler at the edges
Add rod at the edges; correct angle and heat
Burn-through and excess penetration
Nozzle too big; gap too wide; travel too slow
Correct nozzle, gap and speed
Crater crack
Flame pulled off suddenly at the end
Fill the crater; draw the flame away slowly
Distortion
Too much heat; too few tacks; poor order
See the distortion methods

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: Bend test (face and root)
A strip cut across the weld is bent round a former, with the face or the root on the outside
Lack of fusion, porosity and poor penetration open up as cracks
Nick-break test
The weld is saw-notched and broken open
Gas holes and unfused areas on the broken face
Macro test
A cut face is smoothed and etched with a mild acid
The weld's shape, fusion and penetration
Fillet break test
A fillet weld is bent over until it breaks, with the root in tension
Whether the root is fused into both plates; holes in the weld

blocks.p: In a fillet break, a sound weld usually breaks through its throat, showing clean, fused metal right into the root corner of both plates. A smooth unfused face against one plate, or a dry corner at the root, shows lack of fusion.

blocks.h: Leak tests for tanks and trays

ul: **Water test:** fill with water, stand it on a dry surface and look for drips or damp patches along every seam.

**Chalk and paraffin test:** paint the outside of the seams with a chalk wash and let it dry; brush paraffin (kerosene) on the inside. Paraffin creeps through even a tiny pinhole and stains the white chalk, marking the leak. Keep the paraffin away from any flame and clean it off before welding again.
Mark every leak, re-weld it, and test again.
Watch for unsafe acts and stop them at once: lit torches hung on cylinders, leaks hunted with a flame, oxygen used for cooling, wrong lighting order, missing goggles.
When a trainee's welds have a fault, **coach**: show the correct method, watch the trainee try it, then check the result together. Repeat until it is right.
Check the first weld of each trainee against the WPS before letting them carry on.
**Weld record:** who welded each joint, the nozzle, pressures, flame and rod used, and the test results, so the work can be traced if a problem shows up later.
**Job record:** gas and rod used, time taken, problems and how they were solved. Compare gas used with the plan: a big overuse points to leaks, idle flames left burning or wrong nozzle sizes.
**Faulty equipment:** tag it, take it out of use and report it in writing.
**Injuries and near misses**, even small burns: give first aid, record them, and find and fix the cause.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can read welding symbols and plan a gas welding job, including the gas, rod and time it needs.
I can write or check a WPS for an oxy-acetylene weld and make sure it is followed.
I can explain why acetylene must be kept below about 1 bar and drawn no faster than the supplier allows, and work out how many cylinders to couple.
I can handle, store and transport cylinders safely.
I can explain how regulators, arrestors, check valves and injector and equal-pressure torches work.
I can test a set for leaks and creep, and take faulty parts out of use.
I can light up and shut down safely, and act correctly on a backfire, flashback or heated cylinder.
I can explain how the flame burns and set neutral, carburising and oxidising flames for the right jobs.
I can choose and use the leftward or rightward method and the right edge preparation for the thickness.
I can weld in the flat, horizontal, vertical and overhead positions, and weld small-bore pipe rolled and fixed.
I can control and correct distortion.
I can weld or braze-weld cast iron, weld aluminium, and deal safely with galvanised steel.
I can inspect gas welds, name defects with their causes and cures, and carry out bend, nick-break, macro, fillet break and leak tests.
I can supervise and coach trainees and keep weld, job and incident records.

terms: Backfire
The flame going out with a bang at the nozzle
Braze welding
Joining with a brass or bronze rod that melts below the parent metal, built up like a weld
Carburising flame
A flame with excess acetylene, showing a white feather
Chill bar
A copper or steel bar clamped beside a seam to draw heat away
Creep
A regulator's working pressure rising with the torch shut, because its seat leaks
Flame-stop element
The part of a flashback arrestor that puts out a flame passing back through it
Flashback
The flame burning back into the hoses or regulator
Flashback arrestor
A safety device at the regulator outlet that stops flashbacks and reverse gas flow
Heat-affected zone (HAZ)
Metal beside the weld changed by heat but not melted
Injector torch
A torch in which an oxygen jet draws the fuel gas through
Leftward welding
Forehand welding: the flame points ahead and the rod leads
Manifold
A set of cylinders joined to feed one supply line
Mixing chamber
The part of the torch where oxygen and acetylene meet and mix
Neutral flame
A flame with balanced oxygen and acetylene and no feather
Nick-break test
Breaking a notched weld to look inside it
Oxidising flame
A flame with excess oxygen and a short, pointed cone
Planishing
Hammering on a dolly to stretch shrunk metal back into shape
Rightward welding
Backhand welding: the flame points back over the weld and the rod follows
Root face
The flat, unbevelled strip along the bottom edge of a V preparation
Spark lighter
The flint lighter used to light a gas torch
Two-stage regulator
A regulator that holds working pressure steady as the cylinder empties
Withdrawal rate
How fast acetylene may safely be drawn from a cylinder

c1.title: Gas supply for heating work in Linstead
c1.text: A shop in Linstead, St Catherine, has a job that needs a large heating nozzle using about 1 800 litres of acetylene an hour. Each acetylene cylinder holds about 7 000 litres, and the supplier's leaflet says to draw no more than one-seventh of the contents per hour. A worker offers to make a manifold from copper water pipe left over from a plumbing job. During the morning check, one acetylene regulator's working-pressure gauge keeps rising slowly while the torch valves are shut.

c2.title: A cracked pump housing in Morant Bay
c2.text: A farmer in Morant Bay, St Thomas, brings in a grey cast iron water-pump housing with an 80 mm crack running in from one flange. The pump does not run hot. The team leader, Nicole, must choose between fusion welding with cast iron rod and braze welding with bronze rod, and plan the preheat and cooling.

c3.title: Duct panels and a trough in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: A bakery in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, orders ducting made from 1 mm mild steel sheet and a small steel water trough for its yard. After the first duct panel is welded, there is a shallow buckle beside the seam. The trough must not leak, and the bakery wants proof before it is delivered.

c4.title: Supervising trainees at a centre in Falmouth
c4.text: Rohan, a Level 3 trainee, is supervising a gas bay at a training centre in Falmouth, Trelawny, where trainees are welding 3 mm and 5 mm steel plate. One trainee is wearing the shade 12 lens from his arc welding helmet. Another cannot get the nut on a new red hose to screw onto the oxygen regulator. A third is passing a lighter round the hose joints to look for leaks. A fourth keeps producing welds with lack of fusion along one edge.

c5.title: Trial fillet welds in Bull Bay
c5.text: At a small shop in Bull Bay, St Andrew, Garfield gas welds trial tee joints of a 3 mm upright plate on a 10 mm base plate for a set of brackets, then breaks them open in a vice to check them.

questions.q: How many acetylene cylinders must be coupled, at least, to supply the heating nozzle?
questions.why: One cylinder may give 7 000 ÷ 7 = 1 000 litres an hour. The nozzle needs 1 800 litres an hour: 1 800 ÷ 1 000 = 1.8, so round up to 2 cylinders on an approved manifold.

questions.q: What is wrong with the worker's offer to make a manifold?
o: Copper pipe is too weak to hold the acetylene cylinder pressure
Acetylene forms explosive compounds with copper
Copper pipe would make the flame burn too hot to control
Copper pipe must be painted red before it carries fuel gas
questions.why: Acetylene reacts with copper (and high-copper alloys, silver and mercury) to form acetylides that can explode on a knock. Manifolds are approved systems with the right materials, arrestors and non-return valves, never home-made.

questions.q: What does the rising working-pressure gauge show, and what should happen?
o: The cylinder is overfilled; open the torch to let some gas out
The gauge needle is sticking; tap the glass and carry on
The hose is too long; fit a shorter hose to that regulator
The regulator seat is leaking; tag it and take it out of use
questions.why: A working pressure that keeps rising with the torch shut is creep: gas is leaking past the regulator seat. The pressure can climb above the safe acetylene limit, so the regulator is tagged, taken out of use and reported.

questions.q: Before welding the crack, why should a small hole be drilled just beyond its end?
o: To stop the crack running further as the casting heats
To let gas escape from inside the housing during welding
To give the flux somewhere to collect away from the weld
To check how thick the casting is at the end of the crack
questions.why: Heating and cooling a cracked casting can make the crack run on. A hole just past the visible end stops it, and the hole is filled as part of the repair.

questions.q: Nicole chooses to braze weld the housing with bronze rod. Which flame should be used?
o: Strongly carburising, to add carbon to the cast iron
Slightly oxidising, to cut fuming from the rod
Strongly oxidising, to burn the graphite out first
Neutral, exactly as for fusion welding steel
questions.why: Bronze (brass) rod contains zinc, which boils off as fume in a neutral flame. A slightly oxidising flame forms a thin oxide film that holds the zinc back, giving a sounder deposit.

questions.q: How should the housing be cooled after the repair?
o: In still air on a cold steel bench
With a gentle spray of water to stop it distorting
Slowly, buried in dry sand or under a heat blanket
With compressed air blown over the repair
questions.why: Cast iron cracks if it cools unevenly or fast. Burying it in dry sand or lime, or wrapping it in a heat blanket, lets the whole casting cool slowly and evenly.

questions.q: Which edge preparation suits a butt joint in the 1 mm sheet?
o: A single-V of about 80°, with a small root gap
Square edges set about 3 mm apart for the filler rod
A single-V of about 60°, with a root face and gap
Edges turned up and melted down with no filler
questions.why: For very thin sheet (up to about 1.5 mm), flanged edges are melted down to form the weld without filler. A V or a wide gap in 1 mm sheet would simply burn through.

questions.q: How can the shallow buckle beside the seam best be taken out?
o: Weld a second run along the seam to pull it flat
Planish it on a dolly, or heat-shrink spots
Heat the whole panel red and quench it in water
Leave it, as the duct brackets will pull it flat
questions.why: Planishing stretches the shrunk area back, and heating small spots on the bulge lets them shrink and pull the panel flat. More welding or quenching would add distortion.

questions.q: For a chalk and paraffin test on the trough, why is chalk wash put on one side of the seams and paraffin on the other?
o: Paraffin seeps through any pinhole and stains the chalk
The chalk soaks up the paraffin and seals the small holes
The paraffin cleans the seams so the chalk shows the cracks
The chalk stops the paraffin catching fire during the test
questions.why: Paraffin (kerosene) creeps through even tiny pinholes that water might not show at once. Where it comes through, it stains the white chalk, marking the leak for re-welding.

questions.q: What filter shade should the trainee wearing the shade 12 lens be using for this gas welding?
o: Shade 2
Shade 5
Shade 10
Shade 13
questions.why: Gas welding of steel usually needs about shade 4 to 6 from the chart. Shade 12 is for arc welding and is far too dark to see the pool, while shade 2 gives too little protection from the glare.

questions.q: Why will the nut on the new red hose not screw onto the oxygen regulator?
o: The nut has rusted and needs a little oil on its thread first
The hose is new and must be warmed in the sun before fitting
Fuel gas nuts are left-handed, so they cannot go on oxygen
The regulator outlet needs tape wrapped round its thread first
questions.why: Red hose is for fuel gas, whose fittings have a left-hand thread and a groove or notch. This stops a fuel hose being fitted to oxygen. He needs the blue (oxygen) hose, and no oil or tape is ever used on gas fittings.

questions.q: What should Rohan do about the trainee using a lighter on the hose joints?
o: Let him carry on, as long as he keeps the flame small
Tell him to use a spark lighter, which is safer
Ask him to switch to a torch so he can see better
Stop him and have him use leak-test solution
questions.why: A flame held to a leaking fuel gas joint can ignite the gas and cause a fire or a flashback. Leaks are found with leak-test solution or soapy water: bubbles show the leak.

questions.q: How should Rohan help the trainee whose welds keep showing lack of fusion along one edge?
o: Tell him to turn up both gas pressures and try again at once
Show the method, watch him weld, then check it with him
Give him a bigger nozzle so the edges melt more easily
Weld the next joint for him so his record looks better
questions.why: Coaching works best as show, try, check: demonstrate melting both edges before adding rod, watch the trainee do it, then look at the result together. Changing pressures or nozzles away from the WPS is not the cure.

questions.q: One broken fillet shows the weld fused into the upright plate, but a dry, unfused corner against the base plate. What should Garfield change?
o: Aim more of the flame at the thick base plate
Aim more of the flame at the thin upright plate
Use a thinner filler rod so it melts sooner
Weld faster so less heat goes into the upright
questions.why: The 10 mm base plate draws heat away much faster than the 3 mm upright, so it did not melt at the root. Directing more heat at the thicker plate brings both up to melting together.

questions.q: Another trial fillet breaks through the throat, showing clean, fused metal right into the root corner of both plates and no holes. What does this show?
o: Lack of root fusion on both plates
A carburising flame was used throughout
The weld is too small for the joint
A sound weld with good root fusion
questions.why: A fillet that breaks through its throat with fusion into the root of both plates and no porosity is what a sound weld looks like in a fillet break test.

questions.q: When gas welding aluminium, what is the main job of the flux?
o: To dissolve the oxide skin so the metal can fuse
To make the aluminium change colour before it melts
To cool the pool so it does not drop through
To add strength to the finished weld metal
questions.why: Aluminium's oxide melts at about 2 050 °C, far above the metal's 660 °C. The flux dissolves the oxide so the pool can fuse. Afterwards every trace must be washed off, or it corrodes the job.

questions.q: A team's gas use for the week is 30% above what the job plan allowed. What should the team leader check first?
o: Whether the plan should simply be raised by 30% for next time
Whether the supplier filled the cylinders properly
Whether there are leaks, idle flames or wrong nozzle sizes
Whether the trainees are welding too slowly on purpose
questions.why: Leaking joints and hoses, torches left burning between jobs and oversized nozzles all waste gas, and leaks are also a fire risk. Check those before changing the plan or blaming the supply.

questions.q: A small-bore steel pipe joint can be either rolled or welded fixed. Why is rolling it usually better?
o: The root needs no penetration on a rolled joint
Most of the joint is welded on top, in the flat
A rolled joint needs no tack welds to hold it
Rolling cools the pipe so it does not distort
questions.why: Turning the pipe keeps the pool on top, in the easiest position, so it is quicker and fuses more reliably. Fixed joints are left for where the pipe cannot be turned.

questions.q: Why is each hose purged for a few seconds before the torch is lit?
o: To warm the nozzle so it does not backfire
To blow dust off the outside of the torch
To test that the flashback arrestors are working
To clear air or mixed gas out of the hoses
questions.why: Air or a mixture of gases left in a hose can burn back when the torch is lit. Purging each hose separately, in a ventilated place away from flames, leaves only the right gas in each line.

questions.q: Compared with an arc weld on the same steel sheet, a gas weld usually has which of these?
o: A narrower heat-affected zone and less distortion
A wider heat-affected zone and more distortion
Deeper penetration and a narrower bead
No heat-affected zone, since no current flows
questions.why: The gas flame is less concentrated and heats a wider band more slowly, so more metal is changed by heat and more shrinks as it cools. That is why distortion control matters so much in gas welding.
